title: The anchoress's window
hook: Julian lived through plague and revolt, and gave counsel through a window to passers-by

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Death, when some fled and some stayed with the sick, and your line was some stayed.

A woman from the town of Lynn has come to stand outside a church in Norwich. She is restless, loud in her weeping, and not everyone trusts her. She has visions, she says, and she wants to know whether they come from God or from somewhere else. She doesn't knock on a door. She goes to a window in the wall of a small cell built onto the church, and speaks to the woman inside, who will never come out. The visitor is Margery Kempe. The woman behind the window is the one we call Julian.

On day two hundred seventy-one we met Julian in her cell, and the visions she wrote down. Today, look the other way, out through the window toward the street. Julian's world wasn't quiet. She lived, tradition says, through years of plague and uprising, when angry crowds marched and the powerful struck back. All of that went on outside her wall, and people came to her window carrying it. We know of one visit because Margery Kempe told it in her own book. Margery describes talking with Julian over several days, pouring out her visions, her tears, the things God seemed to be asking of her. Julian's answer, as Margery remembers it, is careful and kind. Paraphrased: test these stirrings by whether they lead you toward the love of God and of your neighbor. The Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity. Be patient, and don't be shaken by what people say about you. That echoes the First Letter of John, in the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God". Julian didn't tell Margery she was a saint, or a fraud. She gave her a way to tell for herself. And notice what the window asked of Julian. She couldn't go out and fix anyone's life; she could only listen, and answer. Proverbs puts the other side plainly: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." At the window, hearing came first.

Choose one person who might need to talk, a friend going through something, a relative whose calls you let ring, and imagine listening the way Julian did: not fixing, not jumping in, hearing the whole thing. Notice where you'd usually interrupt, and let that urge pass. If you pray, hold them in prayer; if not, hold their voice in mind.
Julian. The anchoress of Norwich who listened and gave counsel through the window of her cell to visitors like Margery Kempe.
Your line: counsel at the window. Not fixing, just hearing the whole matter. That's eight hundred thirty days.

howItsDone: Christians in several traditions seek out spiritual direction, a regular conversation with an experienced listener about prayer and life, and Julian is sometimes remembered as an early example of that kind of counsel.

fork.setup: you're Julian. a restless visitor at your window pours out visions and tears, and asks whether they come from God. what do you say?
options: tell her she's clearly a saint.
tell her she's imagining it and should go home.
give her a way to test it: does it lead to love of God and neighbor?
fork.reveal: as Margery remembers it, Julian told her the Holy Spirit never moves anyone against charity, and to be patient.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman shut away from the world.
what it means: a woman shut in with a window open to it, listening to whoever came, in years of plague and uprising.
what a scholar hears: The Book of Margery Kempe, which records Julian's counsel to test spirits by charity, much like 1 John 4:1.

options: Julian's test: do they lead you toward love of God and neighbor? The Spirit never moves against charity.

Julian said to wait for a sign in the sky before trusting any vision or feeling at all.

notes: Angle chosen to avoid y1 days 271–273 (anchoress, hazelnut, all shall be well): today is the street side of the window and Julian's counsel to Margery.
Claims rule: 'plague and uprising' rests on the index hook (the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 is not named or dated). 'Her book was written in years of plague' is general history; confirm or soften.

Margery's account (Book I, ch. 18): 'over several days' for the 'many days' of holy conversation; the counsel (test by love of God and neighbor; the Holy Spirit never moves against charity; patience; do not fear the world's talk) is paraphrased. Confirm against the text.
Margery dictated her book to scribes; 'told it in her own book' is meant loosely.
howItsDone links Julian to spiritual direction; 'in many churches' and 'often remembered' are soft claims; trim if needed.
